content.title: About
content.content: Bagel chips are crunchy slices made from traditional bagels, baked or fried until golden. They retain the characteristic sesame and poppy seed aroma of a classic bagel, with a subtle sweet note. The product is convenient as a standalone snack or as a complement to dips.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bagel chips are produced from whole bagels that are sliced thin and then baked or fried.
Unlike regular potato chips, they contain more whole grains and are often enriched with sesame, poppy or flax seeds.
In the United States, bagel chips gained popularity in the early 2000s as an alternative to traditional potato chips.
There are many flavor variations: classic, cheese, herb‑spiced, and even sweet cinnamon.

items.title: Rich in whole grains
items.content: Made with whole wheat flour, they provide dietary fiber and complex carbohydrates.

items.title: Contains seeds
items.content: Sesame and poppy seeds add healthy fats, vitamin E, and minerals.

items.title: Low in trans fats
items.content: When baked, the product contains minimal trans‑fat.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: Fiber and protein help keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The product is made from wheat flour and is not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some varieties can be heavily salted; those monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt options.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: While less calorie‑dense than regular chips, bagel chips still provide a notable amount of energy.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bagel chips can be enjoyed as a snack on their own, served with dip sauces, guacamole, hummus, or used as a crunchy topping for salads and soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep refrigerated to maintain crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Chinese pancake (jianbing) is a thin batter made from wheat flour, water, eggs and sometimes added ingredients such as scallions or sesame seeds. The batter is quickly fried on a hot griddle until golden, staying soft inside. It is often served as a snack, side dish, or wrap base.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The traditional Chinese pancake originated in Shandong province and spread throughout the country.
There are many variations: filled with meat, vegetables, seafood or served plain.
Street vendors often fold the pancake into a pocket and serve it with soy sauce, vinegar and chili.
The thinness of the batter allows rapid cooking of large batches, making it ideal for mass service.
In Japan a similar dish called "okonomiyaki" exists, but it has a thicker batter.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: The pancake provides a quick source of energy through easily digestible carbs.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Eggs add both animal and plant protein, supporting tissue repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When cooked with minimal oil, the pancake remains a low‑calorie option.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat flour and eggs supply thiamine, riboflavin and niacin, which aid metabolism.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: The batter contains iron, magnesium and phosphorus, important for bones and blood.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat flour can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Eggs in the batter may cause allergic responses.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: The pancake can raise blood sugar quickly, so diabetics should monitor portion size.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: When served with soy sauce or added salt, the dish can become overly salty.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chinese pancake is served hot, rolled or folded into a pocket. It can be filled with stir‑fried meat, vegetables, tofu, hoisin sauce, or simply sprinkled with scallions and sesame seeds. Common accompaniments are soy sauce, vinegar and spicy chili sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh pancakes are best eaten immediately, but they can be kept in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a zip‑lock bag at –18 °C and reheat in a microwave or skillet before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit cocktail in syrup is a mixture of diced fruits (typically pineapple, peach, pear, cherry and orange) preserved in a sweet sugar syrup. The product is produced by hot sterilization, giving it a long shelf‑life without refrigeration.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Canned fruit cocktail is often used as a quick ingredient for desserts, salads and drinks.
The syrup usually contains about 20‑30 % sugar, which helps retain the bright colour and aroma of the fruits.
In the former Soviet Union a similar product was called “fruit mix in syrup” and was popular in school cafeterias.
Most manufacturers add a small amount of citric acid to stabilise flavour and prevent fruit darkening.
Fruit cocktail is frequently used as a base for homemade ice cream and fruit jellies.

items.title: Source of Vitamin C
items.content: The fruits retain some vitamin C, which supports the immune system and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Dietary Fiber
items.content: Fiber content aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Low Fat
items.content: The product contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The syrup provides additional liquid, useful during periods of increased fluid loss.

items.title: High Sugar Content
items.content: The syrup is high in sugar, so consumption should be moderate, especially for people with diabetes or those watching their weight.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some brands use preservatives such as potassium sorbate, which may cause allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Bisphenol A in Cans
items.content: Long‑term storage in metal cans can lead to BPA migration; choosing BPA‑free or glass packaging is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fruit cocktail can be eaten straight from the jar, added to yogurt, oatmeal, muesli, used as a filling for pancakes, pies and cakes, or blended into smoothies and cocktails. Draining part of the syrup is recommended for a less sweet version.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 3‑5 days. Discard if any off‑odor or colour change occurs.

content.title: About
content.content: Dry milk is a dehydrated dairy product obtained by evaporating water from whole milk or its components. It retains most nutrients, stores easily, and reconstitutes quickly with water to produce liquid milk when needed.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dry milk was used in expeditions and military campaigns because of its long shelf life.
The first commercial process for producing dry milk was developed in the early 20th century in the United States.
It is often added to confectionery, sauces, and infant formulas to improve flavor and nutritional value.
In some countries dry milk is an important calcium source where fresh milk is scarce.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Dry milk provides a high amount of calcium, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: It contains all essential amino acids, making it a complete protein source.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Dry milk retains vitamins B2, B12 and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Convenient storage
items.content: Lack of moisture allows long‑term storage without refrigeration while preserving nutrients.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Dry milk contains lactose, so individuals with intolerance should choose lactose‑free alternatives.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey may experience reactions.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Some dry milks are sweetened; check the label if you need to limit sugar.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: To reconstitute, dissolve 1 part dry milk in 4–5 parts cold water, stirring thoroughly. Add dry milk to dough, sauces, cereals, coffee or tea to enhance flavor and nutrition.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry milk in a sealed container in a cool, dry place away from direct light. After opening, use within 6–12 months for best quality.

content.title: About
content.content: Shrimp, cake or patty (1363) is a ready‑to‑eat seafood product formed into small patties. The shrimp is peeled, minced, mixed with breadcrumbs, spices and sometimes egg, then shaped into a patty and cooked by steaming, frying or baking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Shrimp is one of the fastest‑growing seafood species and can be farmed in aquaculture.
Shrimp patties are popular in Asian cuisines, especially in Japan (tempura) and Thailand (krato).
Shrimp provides more protein per weight than most fish varieties.
Shrimp gets its pink hue from astaxanthin, a powerful antioxidant.
Patty‑style shrimp cakes are convenient for storage and microwave reheating.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Shrimp contains about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many meat patties, shrimp patties have low saturated fat content.

items.title: Provides iodine and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals are essential for thyroid function and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Contains astaxanthin
items.content: Astaxanthin offers strong antioxidant benefits for eye and skin health.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Low cholesterol and the presence of omega‑3 fatty acids favor cardiovascular health.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Shrimp contains moderate cholesterol; people with hypercholesterolemia should monitor portion size.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Prepared patties often contain added salt; choose low‑sodium versions if you have hypertension.

items.title: Food additives
items.content: Some manufacturers add preservatives and flavor enhancers that may be undesirable for sensitive consumers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Shrimp patties can be enjoyed hot or cold, added to salads, soups, burgers, or served with tartar sauce, soy sauce, or lemon juice. They reheat well on a skillet, in the oven, or in a microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the product refrigerated at 0–4 °C in its original packaging and consume within 3 days after opening. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 2 months. Discard if an off‑odor or discoloration appears.

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese strudel is a pastry made from thin, flaky dough filled with a creamy cheese mixture, often enriched with raisins, candied peel or vanilla. The dough is crisp, while the filling is soft and mildly sweet.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The strudel tradition originated in Austria, but in Russia it is commonly prepared with cottage cheese.
The thin dough is made from flour, eggs, butter and a small amount of water, giving it great elasticity.
The cheese filling may include cottage cheese, cream cheese, and sometimes lemon zest for aroma.
Strudel is usually served warm, dusted with powdered sugar or drizzled with melted butter.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Cottage cheese provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The cheese filling supplies calcium important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cottage cheese contains vitamins B2 and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Low added sugar
items.content: When modest amounts of sugar are used, strudel can be more balanced in carbs than many sweet pastries.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: If fermented cheese is used, it may contain beneficial bacteria for gut health.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The cheese filling contains lactose, which can cause discomfort for lactose‑intolerant individuals.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: People allergic to milk or dairy products should avoid this pastry.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: The buttery dough makes the strudel energy‑dense, so portion control is recommended.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Excessive sugar in the filling raises the glycemic index of the product.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve cheese strudel warm, sliced into portions. It can be dusted with powdered sugar, drizzled with melted butter, or accompanied by a berry sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the strudel in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, refrigerate up to 5 days or freeze for up to 2 months.
